title: How Two Bengaluru Founders Turned Surplus Milk Into a 50-Store Mithai Chain
excerpt: Shwetha Rajashekar and Vishwanath Murthy built India Sweet House from their Karma Farms dairy after spotting a gap for premium, hygienic mithai - with FY25 revenue of Rs 83.10 crore in Tracxn data cited by Moneycontrol.
body:
• Bengaluru entrepreneurs Shwetha Rajashekar and Vishwanath Murthy built India Sweet House from Karma Farms, their organic dairy farm near Bengaluru, after surplus milk became hard to sell during the pandemic.
  • The mithai chain has grown to more than 50 outlets across Karnataka in about four years, selling sweets made with milk, khova and ghee from its own farm.
  • Financial data cited by Moneycontrol from Tracxn put revenue at Rs 83.10 crore in FY25, with Rs 6.15 crore EBITDA and Rs 1.83 crore net profit - below the Rs 100 crore figure in some headline coverage, so treat that larger number as a reported claim, not an audited result.
  • For diaspora readers: the brand says it is exploring export channels for traditional sweets, but its stores remain concentrated in Karnataka for now.

Shwetha Rajashekar saw the gap plainly. In her words to Global Indian: “We saw a gap in the market for premium, hygienic, and beautifully crafted Indian sweets that celebrated authenticity yet appealed to contemporary sensibilities.” Around 2021, she and her co-founder conceptualised India Sweet House, a brand meant to reimagine Indian mithai for the modern consumer without losing its traditional base.

From surplus milk to sweets

The business did not start as a sweet shop. According to reporting cited from Moneycontrol, the founders ran Karma Farms, an organic dairy enterprise spanning more than 20 acres near Bengaluru. Selling liquid milk brought thin margins, distribution problems and, during the disruptions of 2020, surplus milk that could not be cleared through wholesale channels. Converting that milk into khova, desi ghee and paneer - and then into sweets - moved the same raw material into higher-value products.

Dairy News 7x7, summarising the Moneycontrol reporting, says India Sweet House was established in 2020, began with an online-first model through platforms including BigBasket, and opened its first physical outlet in Bengaluru's Malleswaram in 2021. The farm connection stayed central: the brand says its sweets are made using milk, khova and organic ghee sourced from its farm, which operates an automated milking parlour.

"We saw a gap in the market for premium, hygienic, and beautifully crafted Indian sweets that celebrated authenticity yet appealed to contemporary sensibilities."

- Shwetha Rajashekar, co-founder, India Sweet House, to Global Indian

What the chain sells

Global Indian names the Special Ghee Mysore Pak, made with slow-roasted gram flour and pure desi ghee, and the Jaggery Kaju Katli and Rose Pistachio Laddoo among its bestsellers. Presentation is part of the pitch: sweets are boxed for gifting, aiming to lift mithai to the same shelf as premium global desserts. Other coverage notes a wider range that extends beyond sweets into savouries and snacks, and a revival of Chandrahara, a quarter-moon-shaped Karnataka sweet served on rabdi and offered on Sundays.

The numbers, with their sources

The growth is real, but the exact turnover depends on which report you read. Dairy News 7x7 cites Moneycontrol data from Tracxn showing Rs 83.10 crore in revenue in FY25, Rs 6.15 crore in EBITDA and Rs 1.83 crore in net profit, and a $1 million raise from Viney Equity Market in October 2024 described as a pre-IPO raise. A separate dairy-industry report put annual turnover at about Rs 80 crore as the chain reached 50 stores. Some newer headline coverage frames the business as a Rs 100 crore success. Readers should treat the Tracxn-based FY25 figure as the sourced financial baseline and the larger figure as an unattributed headline claim until the company publishes updated financials.

People and next steps

Shwetha brings a corporate background to the venture: she told Global Indian she began at Goldman Sachs in Bengaluru in 2008 and later spent more than five years at Tesco HSC in global sourcing and business analytics. India Sweet House says women play strong roles across production, design and retail. One industry report put the workforce at more than 800 people, primarily rural women.

The chain's stated direction is geographic expansion beyond Karnataka and, according to industry reporting, exploration of export channels aimed at diaspora demand for traditional sweets. No export launch date or overseas store has been announced in the sources for this article, so diaspora readers in the United States should not expect a local outlet yet - the story, for now, is a Karnataka retail chain built by turning a dairy problem into a branded mithai business.
